one_paragraph_summary: With the denial of her MR and the affirmation of the 8-6 May 11 judgment (per J. Tijam) ousting her -- the decision DISQUALIFYING, finding GUILTY, and OUSTING her -- Panganiban lays out Sereno's four post-ouster options. She still has an arguable claim that the judgment is void ab initio for having been rendered by a prejudged, biased majority without due process, and at 58 (turning on July 2) she had a 12-year remaining CJ term to 2030 -- potentially restored if the Court's composition changes. But a Senate run would be deemed a waiver of that claim (as Miriam Santiago's Senate win waived her presidential protest, and CJ Fernan had to leave the Court to run for president/VP in 1992). She was not barred from future public office by the QW ouster -- unlike impeachment which carries that disqualification. A third option of continuing public advocacy preserves the CJ claim but exposes her to further punitive action: the show-cause order for violating the Code of Professional Responsibility, the Code of Judicial Conduct, the sub judice rule, and casting aspersions on the Court members; potential criminal and civil cases under the RPC and NIRC; and possible disbarment or contempt. Fading away quietly preserves her from further lashing, but accepting retirement benefits -- substantial, given her combined ~28 years of UP professorship and Court service, entitling her to lifetime incumbent's pay extending to her spouse -- would itself constitute a waiver of any remaining CJ claim. The column closes with the scriptural 'Quo vadis?' -- Peter's apocryphal question to the risen Jesus -- asking Sereno whether she will return to 'Calvary to be crucified again' or simply fade away. The author notes with restrained retrospective judgment that she lost her more powerful pulpit partly by venturing unwisely into the 'murky political thicket' without securing her colleagues' support, thereby incurring the ire of the 'god of the political plains.'
